questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y),$ traversed along the line segment from $(1,3)$ to $(0,3)?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,3)$ to $(0,3).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+3\,j$ and $b=3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(i+3\,j)+t[3\,j-(i+3\,j)] \\  & =(i+3\,j)-t\,i \\  & =(1-t)\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1-t$ and $y=3$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)j \\  & =-i \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(x+y)$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡((1-t)+3) \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{ln}⁡(4-t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y},$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-3,4)?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-3,4).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=0$ and $b=-3\,i+4\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =0+t\,(b-0) \\  & =t(b) \\  & =t(-3\,i+4\,j) \\  & =-3t\,i+4t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-3t$ and $y=4t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)j \\  & =-3\,i+4\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={e}^{-3t+4t} \\  & ={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\cdot 5\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=1+x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-1,1)$ to $(1,2)?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,1)$ to $(1,2).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+j$ and $b=i+2\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+j)+t[(i+2\,j)-(-i+j)] \\  & =(-i+j)+t(2\,i+j) \\  & =(2t-1)\,i+(t+1)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t-1$ and $y=t+1$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)j \\  & =2\,i+j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=1+x-\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1+(2t-1)-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1) \\  & =2t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))\cdot \sqrt{5}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2t-\operatorname{cos}⁡(t+1))\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,2)$ to $(3,1)?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,2)$ to $(3,1).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=2\,j$ and $b=3\,i+j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =2\,j+t[(3\,i+j)-2\,j] \\  & =2\,j+t(3\,i-j) \\  & =3t\,i+(2-t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=3t$ and $y=2-t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)j \\  & =3\,i-j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+(-1)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3t)^{2}-(2-t) \\  & =9{t}^{2}+t-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}+t-2)\cdot \sqrt{10}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}(9{t}^{2}+t-2)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=2x+y,$ traversed along the line segment from $(-3,1)$ to $(2,3)?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-3,1)$ to $(2,3).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-3\,i+j$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-3\,i+j)+t[(2\,i+3\,j)-(-3\,i+j)] \\  & =(-3\,i+j)+t(5\,i+2\,j) \\  & =(5t-3)\,i+(1+2t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=5t-3$ and $y=1+2t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5t-3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)j \\  & =5\,i+2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{5}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{29}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(5t-3)+(1+2t) \\  & =12t-5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(12t-5)\cdot \sqrt{29}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{29}{\int }_{0}^{1}(12t-5)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi (y-x)}{8})\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(1,1)$ to $(2,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,1)$ to $(2,4).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+j$ and $b=2\,i+4\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(i+j)+t[2\,i+4\,j-(i+j)] \\  & =(i+j)+t(i+3\,j) \\  & =(1+t)\,i+(1+3t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1+t$ and $y=1+3t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)j \\  & =1\,i+3\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{10}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi (y-x)}{8})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi ((1+3t)-(1+t))}{8}) \\  & ={sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{4}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi (y-x)}{8})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{4})\cdot \sqrt{10}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{4})\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\frac{\pi t}{4},$ $\text{d}u=\frac{\pi }{4}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{10}{\int }_{0}^{1}{sec}^{2}⁡(\frac{\pi t}{4})\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}{sec}^{2}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }\operatorname{tan}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }(\operatorname{tan}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4})-\operatorname{tan}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }(1-0) \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{10}}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+\sqrt{2y}$ along the line segment from $(2,0)$ to $(2,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(2,0)$ to $(2,2).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=2\,i$ and $b=2\,i+2\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =2\,i+t[(2\,i+2\,j)-2\,i] \\  & =2\,i+2t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2$ and $y=2t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)j \\  & =2j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+\sqrt{2y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2+\sqrt{2(2t)} \\  & =2+2\sqrt{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2+2\sqrt{t})\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}(1+\sqrt{t})\text{d}t \\  & =4{[t+\frac{2{t}^{3/2}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4(1+\frac{2}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{20}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}(4x+2)\,{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(0,1)$ to $(2,3).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,1)$ to $(2,3).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=j$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =j+t[2\,i+3\,j-j] \\  & =j+t(2\,i+2\,j) \\  & =2t\,i+(1+2t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t$ and $y=1+2t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+2t)j \\  & =2\,i+2\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=(4x+2)\,{e}^{xy}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4(2t)+2){e}^{2t(1+2t)} \\  & =(8t+2)\,{e}^{2t+4{t}^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8t+2)\,{e}^{2t+4{t}^{2}}\cdot 2\sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(8t+2)\,{e}^{2t+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2t+4{t}^{2},$ $\text{d}u=(2+8t)\,\text{d}t$ as follows:  

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(8t+2)\,{e}^{2t+4{t}^{2}}\,\text{d}t & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{6}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\,{e}^{u}\,{|}_{0}^{6} \\  & =2\sqrt{2}({e}^{6}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =2\sqrt{2}({e}^{6}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{3x+y}$ along the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-1,4).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,0)$ to $(-1,4).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=0$ and $b=-i+4\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =0+t\,(b-0) \\  & =t\,(b) \\  & =t(-i+4\,j) \\  & =-t\,i+4t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-t$ and $y=4t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t)j \\  & =-i+4\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{17}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={e}^{3x+y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={e}^{3(-t)+4t} \\  & ={e}^{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\cdot \sqrt{17}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{17}{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{t}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{17}[{e}^{t}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{17}(e-1).\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy$ along the line segment from $(1,2)$ to $(4,7).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,2)$ to $(4,7).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+2\,j$ and $b=4\,i+7j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(i+2\,j)+t[4\,i+7j-(i+2\,j)] \\  & =(i+2\,j)+t(3i+5j) \\  & =(1+3t)\,i+(2+5t)\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1+3t$ and $y=2+5t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+3t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2+5t)j \\  & =3i+5j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{3}^{2}+{5}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{34}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+3t)(2+5t) \\  & =15{t}^{2}+11t+2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(15{t}^{2}+11t+2)\cdot \sqrt{34}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{34}{\int }_{0}^{1}(15{t}^{2}+11t+2)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{34}{[5{t}^{3}+\frac{11}{2}{t}^{2}+2t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{34}(5+\frac{11}{2}+2)-0 \\  & =\frac{25\sqrt{34}}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(1,2,0)$ to $(2,1,3).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from$(1,2,0)$ to $(2,1,3).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i+2\,j$ and $b=2\,i+j+3\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(i+2\,j)+t[(2\,i+j+3\,k)-(i+2\,j)] \\  & =(i+2\,j)+t(i-j+3\,k) \\  & =(1+t)\,i+(2-t)\,j+3t\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1+t,$ $y=2-t,$ and $z=3t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2-t)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3t)k \\  & =i-j+3\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{11}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(1+t)(2-t)^{2} \\  & ={t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+4)\cdot \sqrt{11}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{11}{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{3}-3{t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{11}{[\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}-{t}^{3}+4t]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{11}(\frac{1}{4}-1+4)-0 \\  & =\frac{13\sqrt{11}}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(3,-2,3)$ to $(5,-1,7).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=3i-2\,j+3k$ and $b=5\,i-j+7\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(3i-2\,j+3k)+t[(5\,i-j+7\,k)-(3i-2\,j+3k)] \\  & =(3i-2\,j+3k)+t(2i+\,j+4k) \\  & =(2t+3)\,i+(t-2)\,j+(4t+3)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t+3,y=t-2,$ and $z=4t+3$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4t+3)k \\  & =2i+j+4\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{21}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2x+y-z}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\sqrt{2(2t+3)+(t-2)-(4t+3)} \\  & =\sqrt{t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{t+1}\cdot \sqrt{21}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{21}{\int }_{0}^{1}\sqrt{t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}(x+z))\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(-1,2,1)$ to $(1,2,5).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-1,2,1)$ to $(1,2,5).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-i+2\,j+k$ and $b=i+2\,j+5\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-i+2\,j+k)+t[(i+2\,j+5\,k)-(-i+2\,j+k)] \\  & =(-i+2\,j+k)+t(2\,i+4\,k) \\  & =(-1+2t)\,i+2\,j+(1+4t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-1+2t,$ $y=2,$ and $z=1+4t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-1+2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1+4t)k \\  & =2\,i+0+4\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}+{4}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{20} \\  & =2\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}(x+z))$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}((-1+2t)+(1+4t))) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi t}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{4}(x+z))\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi t}{2})\cdot 2\sqrt{5}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi t}{2})\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=\frac{3\pi t}{2}$, $\text{d}u=\frac{3\pi }{2}\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{3\pi t}{2})\,\text{d}t & =\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{3\pi }{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{3\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡u\,{|}_{0}^{3\pi /2} \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{3\pi }(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{3\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{3\pi }(-1-0) \\  & =-\frac{4\sqrt{5}}{3\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate the integral ${\int }_{C}x{e}^{yz}\,\text{d}s$ along the line segment from $(2,-2,4)$ to $(4,-1,5).$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(2,-2,4)$ to $(4,-1,5).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=2\,i-2\,j+4\,k$ and $b=4\,i-\,j+5\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(2\,i-2\,j+4\,k)+t[(4\,i-\,j+5\,k)-(2\,i-2\,j+4\,k)] \\  & =(2\,i-2\,j+4\,k)+t(2\,i+j+k) \\  & =(2t+2)\,i+(t-2)\,j+(t+4)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t+2,$ $y=t-2,$ and $z=t+4$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+2)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-2)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+4)k \\  & =2\,i+j+k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=x{e}^{yz}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2t+2){e}^{(t-2)(t+4)} \\  & =(2t+2){e}^{{t}^{2}+2t-8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{e}^{yz}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(2t+2){e}^{{t}^{2}+2t-8}\cdot \sqrt{6}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2t+2){e}^{{t}^{2}+2t-8}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u={t}^{2}+2t-8$, $\text{d}u=(2t+2)\,\text{d}t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2t+2){e}^{{t}^{2}+2t-8}\,\text{d}t & =\sqrt{6}\,{\int }_{-8}^{-5}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{6}\,{e}^{u}\,{|}_{-8}^{-5} \\  & =\sqrt{6}({e}^{-5}-{e}^{-8}) \\  & =\sqrt{6}(\frac{1}{{e}^{5}}-\frac{1}{{e}^{8}}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{6}({e}^{3}-1)}{{e}^{8}}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=\frac{y+z}{x},$ traversed along the line segment from $(-4,1,5)$ to $(-2,3,3)?$
questions.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{t}_{a}}^{{t}_{b}}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(-4,1,5)$ to $(-2,3,3).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=-4i+j+5\,k$ and $b=-2\,i+3\,j+3\,k.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(-4i+j+5\,k)+t[(-2\,i+3\,j+3\,k)-(-4i+j+5\,k)] \\  & =(-4i+j+5\,k)+t(2i+2\,j-2\,k) \\  & =(2t-4)\,i+(2t+1)\,j+(5-2t)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t-4,y=2t+1,$ and $z=5-2t$ along the segment.

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t-4)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t+1)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5-2t)k \\  & =2\,i+2\,j-2\,k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-2)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{12} \\  & =2\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y,z)=\frac{y+z}{x}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{(2t+1)+(5-2t)}{2t-4} \\  & =\frac{6}{2t-4} \\  & =\frac{3}{t-2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{t-2}\cdot 2\sqrt{3}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =6\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{t-2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find a definite integral that is equivalent to the line integral of the function $f(x,y) = x+\sin{y},$ traversed along the line segment from $(1,0)$ to $(1,1).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{t_a}^{t_b}  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(1,0)$ to $(1,1).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{i}$ and $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{i}+\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+t[(i+j)-i] \\  & =i+t\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=1$ and $y=t$ along the segment.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t)j \\  & =0\,i+j \\  & =j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{0}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x+\sin{y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Evaluate the integral of the function $f(x,y) = e^{x+y}$ along the line segment from $(0,3)$ to $(2,3).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_{t_a}^{t_b}  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,3)$ to $(2,3).$ 

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=3\,\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b}=2\,\mathbf{i}+3\,\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =3\,j+t[(2\,i+3\,j)-3\,j] \\  & =3\,j+t(2\,i) \\  & =2t\,i+3\,j\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=2t$ and $y=3$ along the segment.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3)j \\  & =2\,i \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = e^{x+y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={e}^{2t+3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t+3}\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t+3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2t+3,$ $\textrm d u=2\,\textrm d t$ as follows: 

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{0}^{1}{e}^{2t+3}\,\text{d}t & ={\int }_{3}^{5}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & ={e}^{u}\,{|}_{3}^{5} \\  & ={e}^{5}-{e}^{3} \\  & ={e}^{3}({e}^{2}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Find the line integral of the function $f(x,y,z) = x^2+y-z,$ traversed along the line segment from $(0,1,-3)$ to $(-1,2,-2)?$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}s  =  \int\limits_{t_a}^{t_b}  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t,
$$

 

where $C$ is the line segment from $(0,1,-3)$ to $(-1,2,-2).$

The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a}=\mathbf{j}-3\mathbf{k}$ and $\mathbf{b}=-\,\mathbf{i}+2\,\mathbf{j}-2\,\mathbf{k}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =(j-3k)+t[(-\,i+2\,j-2\,k)-(j-3k)] \\  & =(j-3k)+t(-i+\,j+k) \\  & =-t\,i+(t+1)\,j+(t-3)\,k\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x=-t, y=t+1,$ and $z=t-3$ along the segment.

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j+\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}\,k \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(-t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t+1)j+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(t-3)k \\  & =-i+j+k \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2+y-z$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(-t)^{2}+(t+1)-(t-3) \\  & ={t}^{2}+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{1}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+4)\cdot \sqrt{3}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}({t}^{2}+4)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$
